rulings.reason: The instruction scores a pedagogical delivery convention -- whether work is left for the asker versus handed over -- so a 10 is evidence about how the solution is packaged, not about whether the mathematics is right, complete, or responsive to the question. Mixed because answerers who deliberately scaffold are plausibly more engaged with the asker's actual difficulty and may write better solutions for that reason.

This scores boilerplate and rhetorical register (disclaimers, apologies, meta-talk about the post) rather than the mathematical content, and a judge applying it would be counting prefatory formulae; the one substantive case it catches, an explicit 'this is not an answer', is incidental to the instruction as written. Mixed because habitual hedging plausibly co-occurs with genuinely thinner or less certain mathematics.

Warmth versus coldness is a tone/community-style marker: an answer can be maximally patient and mathematically wrong, or curt and fully correct, so a high score is not evidence about substance even though it predicts acceptance. Mixed because a patient disposition plausibly travels with more careful and complete exposition.

The instruction scores an etiquette and ordering convention -- affirmation placed before correction -- and can be satisfied by a vacuous 'your work looks fine' without any accurate diagnosis, so it measures presentation order rather than the quality of the correction. Mixed because genuinely diagnosing which steps were right often requires real engagement with the asker's work, which co-produces better answers.
